tip: De-words keep the -e even after 'een': 'een vriendelijke buurman', because 'buurman' is a de-word.
'Half acht' means 7:30, not 8:30: Dutch reads it as half an hour toward eight.
'Zich oriënteren' needs a word pointing back at the subject: 'wij oriënteren ons' = we orient ourselves.
To say have been, Dutch uses 'zijn' (be), not 'hebben' (have): 'wij zijn ... geweest' = we have been.
Comparisons use 'dan' for than: 'groter dan' (taller than). Learners often say 'groter als' by mistake, but standard Dutch is 'dan'.
'Ondanks' means despite and links straight to a noun, no verb: 'ondanks de tegenslagen'.
In Dutch you congratulate someone 'met' (with) a thing, not on it: 'gefeliciteerd met je verjaardag'.
Weather verbs use a placeholder subject 'het': 'het regent' means it rains, with no real thing doing it.
Adjectives usually add -e before a noun: 'schoon' becomes 'schone' in 'een schone kamer'.
Dutch often names the posture of a located thing: upright items 'staan', so 'de hete soep staat op tafel', not just is.
Drop the -e when a neuter (het) noun follows 'een': 'een lief kind', not 'een lieve kind', since it is 'het kind'.
'Opbellen' splits in a main clause: the 'op' part jumps to the end, 'belde haar ouders ... op'.
'Tot' marks until, up to a time or point: 'tot sluitingstijd' means until closing time.
Dutch uses 'lopen' for the course of a path or road: 'het fietspad loopt', literally the bike path walks.
Adjectives double as adverbs with no extra ending: 'stil' covers both quiet and quietly, as in 'viel stil'.
Comparisons use the ending -er plus 'dan' for than: 'comfortabeler dan het harde'.
Around wraps the noun in 'om ... heen', one word each side: 'om het meer heen' means around the lake.
Say by a vehicle with 'met', not a word for by: 'met de auto' means by car.
'Kijken' pairs with 'naar' to mean watch: 'keek naar het journaal' is watched the news.
Direction down something goes after it with 'af': 'de trap af' means down the stairs.
Our is 'ons' before a neuter (het) noun and 'onze' elsewhere: 'ons huis', because it is 'het huis'.
'Doordat' means because for a direct cause or result, often unintended, while 'omdat' gives a reason or motive: 'doordat zij te laat vertrok' (because she left too late).
For the best within a group, Dutch marks the group with 'van', not in: 'het modernste museum van de stad'.
Start with an 'als' clause and the main verb comes right after the comma: 'als je wilt, kun je'.
The Dutch 'half' points to the next hour: 'half acht' means 7:30, half toward eight, not 8:30.
Some units of measure stay singular after a number: 'twee uur' for two hours, not 'twee uren'.
'Of' means whether in an indirect yes-no question: 'weet niet of haar broer morgen komt' = doesn't know whether her brother comes tomorrow.
To say likes doing something, Dutch adds 'graag' to the verb: 'danst graag' means likes to dance.
'Elkaar' means each other, one word for a two-way action: 'elkaar voorstellen', introduce each other.
'Er' works as there in there-are statements: 'er staan zeventig containers' means there are seventy containers.
